summary.title: Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP) Explained
summary.one_liner: RASP is a runtime security technology that watches application behavior in production and blocks malicious actions such as shell execution, file access, or database calls, complementing WAFs.
takeaways: RASP instruments the application at runtime and blocks suspicious actions (e.g., running a shell, opening a file, calling a database) as they happen.
Unlike WAFs, which rely on signatures and sit at the perimeter, RASP sees application behavior and context, which can reduce false positives.
RASP needs no application code changes and can keep protecting apps after perimeter breaches.
RASP works best alongside a broader AppSec program, WAF capabilities, and DevSecOps tooling, and should be performance-tested before deployment.
summary.summary: This Rapid7 fundamentals article explains runtime application self-protection (RASP), defining it using Gartner's description and describing how an agent placed in the server adds security checks to running applications. It contrasts RASP with web application firewalls, noting that WAFs filter traffic at the perimeter using static rules while RASP inspects what the application does with requests. The page closes with three best practices: use RASP as part of a comprehensive AppSec program, evaluate its integration with SIEM, DAST, and ticketing tools, and test it for performance impact before rollout.
